prompt: Of a project's id, name, parent and billing account, which is fixed for the project's whole life?
hint: It is in every resource's name.

choices.text: The billing account, once linked
choices.why: The link can move to another billing account at any time; lesson 11 does it.

choices.text: The id
choices.why: Right. The id never changes and is never reused, so it is the minute to spend care on.

choices.text: The parent folder
choices.why: A project can be moved to another folder, though it rarely is.

choices.text: The name shown in the console
choices.why: The name is a label for people and can be changed whenever you like.

prompt: Which of these is a valid project id?
hint: Lowercase, digits and hyphens, a letter first, no hyphen last.

choices.text: `Planner_Reports`
choices.why: Capitals and underscores are refused, which is exactly what the provider said in the lab.

choices.text: `planner-reports-`
choices.why: A trailing hyphen is the one character an id may not end on.

choices.text: `2026-planner`
choices.why: An id has to start with a letter, so a year in front makes it invalid.

choices.text: `planner-reports-2`
choices.why: Right. It starts with a letter, holds only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, and ends on a digit.

prompt: In the lab, `terraform validate` refused `Planner (reports)` as a project name. Who refused it?
hint: Did any request leave the laptop?

choices.text: The provider, on the laptop
choices.why: Right. The provider knows the naming rules and refuses before a request exists.

choices.text: Google's Resource Manager, which answered 400
choices.why: `validate` sends nothing to anybody. A 400 is what the API would say, later.

choices.text: The emulator, which also checks projects
choices.why: The emulator answers Pub/Sub and knows no projects at all.

choices.text: Terraform itself, which forbids parentheses in strings
choices.why: Terraform accepts any string. The rule belongs to Google, and the provider carries it.

prompt: A developer with the Owner role on a brand-new project calls the Pub/Sub API and is refused with `SERVICE_DISABLED`. What is missing?
hint: The role is the widest there is. What else does a request need?

choices.text: A narrower role, as Owner is refused by Pub/Sub
choices.why: Owner is not refused anywhere for being too broad; the refusal names the service, not the role.

choices.text: A billing account, which every API requires
choices.why: A missing billing account has an error of its own. `SERVICE_DISABLED` is about the API's switch.

choices.text: The API, which is off until enabled in that project
choices.why: Right. An API is enabled per project, and no role switches it on by being held.

choices.text: A quota increase for the new project
choices.why: Going over a quota answers `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`. This request never reached a quota.

prompt: Why does the lesson call an API being off in a project a guardrail as well as a nuisance?
hint: Think about a credential somebody should not have.

choices.text: Disabled APIs are not billed, so the project costs nothing
choices.why: That is true of unused APIs too. The guardrail is about who can use them, not what they cost.

choices.text: Google enables an API only after a security review
choices.why: Enabling is immediate for anybody with the role. No review happens.

choices.text: A leaked credential cannot use what is off
choices.why: Right. What is off cannot be used, by anybody, until somebody with the right role turns it on.

choices.text: An enabled API cannot be disabled again
choices.why: An API can be disabled; it is the first state, off, that does the guarding.

prompt: What is a label's main job in Google Cloud?
hint: Where do labels end up at the end of the month?

choices.text: To be counted, above all in the billing export
choices.why: Right. A label answers whose a cost is, which is the first question finance asks.

choices.text: To decide who may access a resource
choices.why: Anybody who may edit a resource may edit its labels, so a label must never decide access.

choices.text: To choose which firewall rules apply to a machine
choices.why: That is a network tag, a different thing with a similar name.

choices.text: To give a resource a second, readable id
choices.why: Labels can change at any time, which is exactly what an id must not do.

prompt: `gcloud pubsub topics create invoices --labels=team=Planner` is refused. Why?
hint: Look at the value, not the key.

choices.text: The emulator does not accept labels on new topics
choices.why: It accepted two on `reminders`. And this refusal came from `gcloud`, before anything was sent.

choices.text: A key may not be called `team`
choices.why: `team` is a perfectly good key; the same command with `planner` in lowercase succeeds.

choices.text: A topic may carry only one label
choices.why: A resource may carry up to 64 labels.

choices.text: A label value may not hold a capital letter
choices.why: Right. Keys and values alike are lowercase, digits, hyphens and underscores.

prompt: In the lab, `gcloud pubsub topics update reminders --update-labels=...` answers `INVALID_ARGUMENT`. What should you conclude?
hint: Who answered: Google, or the emulator?

choices.text: That labels cannot be changed once a topic exists
choices.why: Against Google the same command updates them in place. This is the emulator's limit.

choices.text: A gap in the emulator, not a rule of Google's
choices.why: Right. The emulator covers part of the API, and its banner says so. The command itself is correct.

choices.text: That `cost-centre` is not a valid key
choices.why: A hyphen is allowed in a key, and the refusal names the update mask, not the key.

choices.text: That the topic must be deleted and created again with the new label
choices.why: That would work around the emulator, and it is not what you would do against Google.

prompt: A team wants an IAM condition that grants a role only on production resources. Should the condition read a label `env=prod`?

choices.text: No: a Resource Manager tag, bound under its own role
choices.why: Right. A label is edited by anyone who edits the resource; a tag is defined and bound under control.

choices.text: Yes, since labels are copied into every request
choices.why: IAM conditions do not read labels, and they should not: a label is too easy to write.

choices.text: Yes, provided the label is set by Terraform
choices.why: Who set it first does not matter; anybody who may edit the resource may set it again.

choices.text: No: it should read a network tag on the resource
choices.why: Network tags are bare words for firewall rules and routes, read by no IAM condition.

prompt: Match each kind of tag to what reads it.
hint: Three names that sound alike, three different readers.

prompt: At most how many labels may a single resource carry?
A request is refused with `429` and `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, and works again a minute later. Which kind of quota was it?
hint: What resets when the minute turns?

choices.text: An allocation quota
choices.why: An allocation quota counts what exists, and waiting a minute frees nothing.

choices.text: A budget, which blocks spending
choices.why: A budget blocks nothing; lesson 12 makes that point at length.

choices.text: A rate quota
choices.why: Right. A rate quota counts requests over time and frees itself as the window moves on.

choices.text: An organisation policy
choices.why: A policy refuses whatever the hour; it does not recover after a minute.

prompt: A project was deleted twelve days ago. What can still be done?

choices.text: Nothing; deletion is immediate
choices.why: Deletion starts a thirty-day clock, and twelve days is well inside it.

choices.text: Restore it with `gcloud projects undelete`
choices.why: Right. For thirty days the project waits in `DELETE_REQUESTED` and can come back whole.

choices.text: Create a new project with the same id
choices.why: The id stays taken, during the thirty days and forever after.

choices.text: Keep using its resources until the thirty days end
choices.why: Everything inside stops serving the moment deletion is requested.

prompt: For how many days after a deletion request can a project be restored?
Why does the project that hosts a shared network carry a lien Google placed itself?
hint: Who else depends on that project?

choices.text: It keeps the network's quota from being lowered
choices.why: A lien guards deletion, not quotas.

choices.text: It moves the network's bill to the organisation
choices.why: Billing stays linked per project; a lien has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: It locks the network's firewall rules
choices.why: The rules can still be changed. Only deleting the project is refused.

choices.text: Other projects depend on it and would be cut off
choices.why: Right. The lien refuses the deletion while other projects depend on the host.

prompt: `terraform destroy` stops on a `google_project` before sending anything. Nobody set `deletion_policy` in the file. Why did it stop?
hint: Remember a value lesson 2's plan showed without anybody writing it.

choices.text: Google placed a lien on every project Terraform creates
choices.why: A lien is refused by Google, after a request. This stopped before any request.

choices.text: The placeholder token cannot delete projects
choices.why: The token would be refused by Google; the stop happened before Google was asked.

choices.text: A project cannot be deleted by Terraform at all
choices.why: With `deletion_policy = "DELETE"` Terraform deletes it like any other resource.

choices.text: The provider defaults it to `PREVENT`
choices.why: Right. Since version 6 a project is protected unless a diff says `DELETE`, which somebody has to read.

prompt: Put a project's life in order, from creation onwards.
items: deleted for good, with the id still taken
trap: Putting the deletion for good right after the request is the slip: the thirty days in between are what make a mistake recoverable.

prompt: A team creates `planner-reports` in a hurry, enables nothing, labels nothing and asks for no quota. On launch day its service fails. Which of the three omissions is the first to stop a request?
hint: One of the three never stops a request at all.

choices.text: The quota that was never raised
choices.why: A quota is counted only once the API is on. It may bite second, never first.

choices.text: The API that was never enabled
choices.why: Right. `SERVICE_DISABLED` comes before any quota is counted, and a missing label stops nothing.

choices.text: The labels that were never set
choices.why: A resource with no labels works perfectly; it is only unclaimed on the bill.

choices.text: The project id chosen in a hurry
choices.why: A hasty id is permanent and possibly ugly, but it stops no request.
